brief: A utensil holder with two bins that is waterproof and dishwasher safe.

requirements.evidence: Two full hex bases, two storeys tall (fused:0,0,0, fused:1,0,0), each with a deep hex-bin-full-x2 bin, so utensils can stand upright. Open faces are capped and the bases are bolted together. The meshes are checked and clear. I couldn't show cutlery in the bins because the fork, knife and spoon props can only lie flat.

The configurator checks fit only, not watertightness. That depends on the material and how it's printed, which I can't check. I used solid (undrained) bins, so the shape is closed, but that doesn't make it waterproof.
The configurator knows nothing about heat or dishwasher resistance. That depends on the filament the user chooses.

finish.summary: I built a two-bin utensil holder: two full hex bases, each two storeys tall, side by side. Each holds a 2-storey-deep full bin (about 160 mm deep), so long utensils can stand upright. Open faces are closed with solid end caps and the joint between the bases is bolted. check_build passes with no issues and the collision check is clear. I couldn't stage cutlery in the bins: the fork and spoon props can only lie flat, not stand. The configurator only checks fit and collisions. Whether the holder is waterproof or dishwasher safe depends on the material and how it's printed, which this tool can't check, so both are unmet.

lines.label: Edge cap · male, two stories tall
M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
